content: A second prefix now joins meN-, and the
two divide the work between them.
meN- points the verb at something.
ber- keeps it at home.
Ibu saya masih berdiri di sana.    Press 1
= My mother is still standing there.
Saya berjalan ke kota setiap pagi.
= I walk into town every morning.
Nothing is being stood and nothing is
being walked. The subject simply does it,
and that is what ber- says.
Before r, and before a root whose first
syllable holds an r, it shortens to be-:
kerja becomes bekerja, never berkerja.

pronunciation_mappings.1: Ibu saya masih berdiri di sana.

content: On a noun, ber- means having it, wearing
it, or going by it.
nama   -> bernama    to be named
dua    -> berdua     the two together
kerja  -> bekerja    to have a job
sepeda -> bersepeda  to go by bike
Saya punya teman yang bernama Siti.
= I have a friend named Siti.
A ber- verb acts on nothing, though a
noun may follow to name the game or the
language: bermain bola, belajar bahasa.
Where a thing is acted upon, use meN-:
Dia berjalan.     = He walks.
Dia membawa tas.  = He carries a bag.
Kamar yang besar itu untuk nenek.
= The big room is for grandmother.
Word for word that is: room YANG big
that, for grandmother.
yang hooks a description onto a noun. It
covers English who, which and that, all
three with the one word.
orang yang baik
= a person who is kind
rumah yang besar
= the house that is big
With a single adjective you may drop it:
rumah besar says the same thing. Keep
yang when the description runs longer.
yang also stands on its own, and then it
means the one that.
Yang besar untuk nenek.
= The big one is for grandmother.
Yang mana? = Which one?
It also carries whole clauses, and that
is where Indonesian sentences get their
length:
Kamar yang ada di lantai dua itu
kosong.
= The room on the first floor is
empty.
Once you can see yang, a long sentence
comes apart cleanly at that word.
Three little words carry almost all the
movement in the language.
di    at, in, on  - no movement
ke    to, towards - movement there
dari  from        - movement away
Saya tinggal di kota ini.
Kami akan pergi ke kota besok.
Salam dari kami di sini.
di is also a prefix, the one that makes a
passive in Tier 3. The space tells them
apart, and it is not optional:
di rumah = at home
dibawa   = is being carried
Never break one; never join the other.
Position words are nouns, not
prepositions. They sit after di, ke or
dari and take the thing behind them.
dalam     the inside     di dalam
atas      the top        di atas
bawah     the underside  di bawah
luar      the outside    di luar
depan     the front      di depan
belakang  the back       di belakang
samping   the side       di samping
tengah    the middle     di tengah
Kunci ada di dalam lemari itu.
= The key is inside that cupboard.
Ada taman di belakang rumah kami.
= There is a garden behind our house.
Adjectives never change shape. A word in
front of them does the comparing.
lebih   more
kurang  less
paling  most
sangat  very
sekali  very (this one goes after)
Buah di pasar lebih murah, Bu.
= Fruit is cheaper at the market.
Gedung ini paling tinggi di kota kami.
= This building is the tallest in our
city.
Saya lapar sekali.
= I am very hungry.
To name the other side of the comparison,
use daripada:
Mobil merah itu lebih mahal daripada
mobil saya.
= That red car is dearer than mine.
For equals, sama dengan:
Umur saya sama dengan umur kamu.
= I am the same age as you.
Two more behave the same way:
terlalu  too      terlalu mahal
cukup    enough   cukup besar
ter- also builds a top form: terbaik, the
best of all. That prefix arrives in Tier
3 with other work to do first.
